# Workload Balance Vs Distance

Minimising total fleet distance and sharing work evenly across vehicles are **different objectives**,
and optimising the first alone reliably produces a fleet where one vehicle does a great deal and
others do very little. A distance-optimal plan has no reason to care that vehicle 3 drives 40 km and
vehicle 11 drives 4 km — the sum is what is scored.

[[multi-depot-vehicle-routing]] in [[optimization-methods]] takes this on directly and pays a
measurable price for fairness.

## ⚠ LBBS is the user's own coinage

The method is called **LBBS — Large Banned Balance Split**. This name is **not a literature term**. It
is the user's own invented method name, confirmed in interview:

> "A teammate's suggested value; LBBS is my own coinage."
> — interview, 2026-07-28

Anyone citing "LBBS" as an established technique is citing this repository. Recorded here explicitly
so the name is never propagated as standard.

## The two levers

**1. Longest-edge ban.** The longest used leg in a solution is put on a ban list and charged a
penalty, which pushes the search away from the single long haul that creates the imbalance. Only the
top *N* longest edges are banned (`banned_top_n = 1` by default) — the ban is a nudge on one leg, not
a constraint set.

**2. LPT trip→vehicle assignment.** Once trips exist, they are assigned to vehicles by
longest-processing-time first rather than round-robin. LPT is the classic greedy makespan heuristic
and it is doing the same job here: put the big items down first so the small ones fill the gaps.

Two designs of this exist side by side and both are kept: **two-phase** (`lbbs2` — a blind GA finds
the ban, then a second GA runs with that ban fixed) and **single-stage integrated**, where the ban
list grows adaptively inside one GA run every `lbbs_update_interval` generations. Neither is deleted
in favour of the other — see [[multiple-solutions-side-by-side]] and
[[keep-the-superseded-version-in-tree]].

## The trade, measured

After the penalty was made proportionate ([[soft-multiplicative-ban-penalty]]), per-vehicle imbalance
— the coefficient of variation of vehicle workload — drops by roughly 90–95%:

| City (large) | Imbalance before | Imbalance after |
|---|---:|---:|
| berlin | 3.698 | **0.318** |
| budapest | 3.704 | **0.203** |
| wroclaw | 3.702 | **0.200** |
| zurich | 3.702 | **0.261** |

The distance cost is small: across the 12 instances `lbbs_tuned` sits within a few percent of the
tuned blind GA, sometimes better (Zurich large 960,974 vs 971,895; Berlin small 209,231 vs 230,170),
sometimes worse. Neither beats greedy on distance at scale, which is the point of
[[blind-baseline-comparison]] and not a failure of the balance objective.

**The honest reading:** the "before" imbalance of 3.70 was largely a scoring artefact, so the ~90%
figure measures fixing a measurement bug at least as much as it measures balancing a fleet. The repo
says this itself rather than reporting the improvement bare — the imbalance was "pinned at ~3.70 for
all 32 operator combos", which is the signature of an artefact, not of a hard problem.

## Why the trade is worth naming

Distance is the objective that is easy to write down; balance is the one a dispatcher actually
complains about. Any fleet objective that is a pure sum is silently indifferent to distribution, and
you only find out when the plan meets people. Recording it as a *trade* rather than as an improvement
keeps both halves visible: roughly a few percent of distance bought a fleet where no vehicle carries
five times its neighbour's load.
